title: Baghdad, 1258
hookLine: Baghdad falls, the caliph is killed, and chronicles say the Tigris ran dark with ink from books

cards: What color is a river after a library has been thrown into it? Later chroniclers had an answer, and people still repeat it. The Tigris, they wrote, ran dark with the ink of books washed off their pages.
Whether it happened exactly that way, historians argue. But nobody had to invent the grief behind it.
The storm from the east had reached the city of the caliphs, a city of mosques, markets, hospitals and libraries on that river. Today: Baghdad.

teach.h: THE CITY OF THE HOUSE OF WISDOM.
teach.b: Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, the city of the House of Wisdom, where scholars gathered and books were copied and translated. Hulagu, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, led the Mongol armies toward it.
The city was besieged, and the walls were breached. The chronicles say the caliph, al-Musta'sim, went out to the Mongol camp to surrender, hoping to save his people.

teach.h: THE CALIPH GOES OUT, AND IS KILLED.
teach.b: The city was sacked anyway, and the caliph was killed.
The accounts differ on how he died, and on almost every number, so the numbers stay where they are, in dispute. Then the river of ink. Notice what people chose to remember.
Not only the dead, though they mourned the dead. The books. Why would that picture last?
The first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in surah al-'Alaq, are a command to read, and they say of Allah, in Pickthall's English: "Who teacheth by the pen."
A whole civilization had grown around that pen: the Qur'an copied by hand, hadith written down, law, poetry, medicine, maps. Losing the books could feel like having the pen knocked out of your hand.
And yet the story didn't end there. Copies existed in other cities. Scholars carried what they knew in memory.
People who could write kept writing.
The river of ink is a picture of loss, and of what a people treasured, because you only grieve like that for something you loved.

how: Muslims treat copies of the Qur'an with care, keeping them clean and high, and the fall of Baghdad is remembered in histories and classrooms as a loss of lives and of learning.

practice: If you can, pick up a book now: a Qur'an, a family Bible, a grandmother's recipe notebook, a school book with someone's name inside the cover.
Feel its weight, and think of who wrote it, who copied or printed it, who kept it until it reached you, then give it one small act of care, like wiping off the dust.
If you pray, thank Allah for the pen and those who carried it; if not, simply hold the book a moment longer before you set it down.

wordCard.voice: Baghdad. The city of the Abbasid caliphs on the Tigris, sacked by Hulagu's army, its caliph killed, and its books, the chronicles say, thrown in the river. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the city's name; where the name itself comes from is debated.
